DEPARTMENT 205 LAW AND MOTION RULINGS


Case Number: 25SMCV06118    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: 205

Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District 

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

 

MILO JEREMIAH SERRANO, et al.,   

  

Plaintiffs, 

v. 

 

LUXE SUNSET LLC,   

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 25SMCV06118 

  

  Date: September 22, 2026 

  

  ORDER RE: 

  DEFENDANTS’ MOTION 

  FOR LEAVE TO FILE CROSS- 

  COMPLAINT  

   

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a personal injury case.  Plaintiffs were guests at the Luxe Sunset Boulevard Hotel.  They went to dinner at a restaurant at the hotel, called Ciracco.  The hotel and restaurant are allegedly owned and/or managed by Defendants Luxe Sunset LLC and E.H. Summit, Inc. 

Plaintiffs requested a highchair with straps for their son, Plaintiff Milo Jeremiah Serrano.  Defendants’ employees advised that a highchair was not available and instead supplied a booster seat.   

Defendants’ employees placed or directed placement of the booster seat on a cushioned dining chair that was not flat or level. The booster seat was not secured to the cushioned chair with appropriate straps, or anti-slip/stability features.  

Shortly after seating, the booster seat tipped, causing Milo to fall and strike his head, resulting in brain injury and a brain bleed which required surgery.   

The operative complaint alleges claims of (1) negligence, (2) premises liability, (3) negligent undertaking, (4) negligent hiring/training/supervision, and (5) negligent infliction of emotional distress.   

This hearing is on Defendants’ motion for leave to file cross-complaint.  Defendants seek to assert claims of equitable indemnity, apportionment of fault, contribution and declaratory relief against Plaintiff Jonathan Bravo (Milo’s father).  Defendants allege that since the filing of their answer, they learned that Plaintiff Bravo was seated next to Milo when Milo fell.  Bravo was also feeding Milo shortly before Milo fell, and Bravo was the one who placed Milo in the booster seat.  There was no opposition filed as of the posting of this tentative ruling.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

Code of Civil Procedure section 428.10, subdivision (b), authorizes a party against whom a cause of action has been asserted to file a cross-complaint alleging a cause of action against a person alleged to be liable thereon, whether or not that person is already a party, when the proposed cause of action “(1) arises out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences as the cause brought against him or (2) asserts a claim, right, or interest in the property or controversy which is the subject of the cause brought against him.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.10, subd. (b).)  

A party may file a cross-complaint against a co-party or another person before the court sets a trial date. (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(b).)  Here, trial has already been set (for November 20, 2028.)  Once a trial date has been set, the party must obtain leave of court, which “may be granted in the interest of justice at any time during the course of the action.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.50(c).)  

DISCUSSION 

Code of Civil Procedure section 426.30¿governs compulsory cross-complaints.¿Subdivision (a)¿of this statute¿provides in relevant part: “[I]f a party against whom a complaint has been filed and served fails to allege in a cross-complaint any related cause of action which (at the time of serving his answer to the complaint) he has against the¿plaintiff, such party may not thereafter in any other action assert against the¿plaintiff¿the related cause of action not pleaded.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 426.30, subd. (a), italics added.) 

Code of Civil Procedure section 428.10¿governs permissive cross-complaints. It provides in relevant part: “A party against whom a cause of action has been asserted . . .¿may¿file a cross-complaint setting forth [¶] . . . [¶] (b) Any cause of action he has against¿a person¿alleged to be liable thereon,¿whether or not such person is already a party to the action, if the cause of action asserted in his cross-complaint (1) arises out of the same transaction, occurrence, or series of transactions or occurrences as the cause brought against him.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 428.10, subd. (b), italics added.) 

Here, Defendants seek to bring claims of indemnity and contribution.  Neither is a compulsory counterclaim.  For statute of limitations purposes, an action for indemnity or equitable contribution does not accrue until payment is made.  (Croskey et al., Cal. Practice Guide: Insurance Litigation (The Rutter Group 2017) ¶ 15:297, p. 15-56; see also Fireman's Fund Ins. Co. v. Sparks Const., Inc. (2004) 114 Cal.App.4th 1135, 1151, 8 Cal. Rptr. 3d 446 [claims for equitable indemnity and contribution did not accrue until joint tortfeasor paid injured party's claim]; Smith v. Parks Manor (1987) 197 Cal. App. 3d 872, 879, 243 Cal. Rptr. 256 [“Where the claim is one for indemnification or contribution, it accrues when the indemnitee or party seeking contribution suffers a loss through payment of a judgment debt (or settlement) or through payment of more than his fair share of damages."].)  Accordingly, Defendants are not obligated to bring claims for indemnity or contribution until after they have made a payment, which means their indemnity and contribution claims cannot be compulsory counterclaims. 

Because the proposed claims are permissive, the standard is not whether Defendants are acting in good faith or bad faith (Code Civ. Proc., §426.50) but whether the amendment is in the interests of justice. (Code Civ. Proc. § 428.50(c).)  Permission to file a permissive cross-complaint is solely within the trial court’s discretion. (Crocker Nat. Bank v. Emerald (1990) 221 Cal.App.3d 852; Orient Handel v. United States Fid. and Guar. Co. (1987) 192 Cal.App.3d 684, 701.) 

On this record, the Court finds that allowing the filing of the proposed cross-complaint is in the interests of justice. The causes of action asserted in the proposed cross-complaint arise out of the same accident as the causes of action in the Complaint.  The interests of efficiency and judicial economy are served by allowing the resolution of all claims between the parties involving this accident in a single proceeding.  Given the liberal policy in allowing amended pleadings and cross-complaints and the close relationship between the claims in the complaint and those in the proposed cross-complaint, the motion is granted. 

CONCLUSION AND ORDER 

   For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ motion for leave to file a cross-complaint.  Defendants are required to file and serve their cross-complaint within 5 days of this Order. 

 
IT IS SO ORDERED.

Case Number: 25SMCV06496    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

MARTIN KEMPE,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

LEON GURVIN, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.:  25SMCV06496 

 

  Hearing Date: September 22, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  DEFENDANT MICHAEL BOCK’S  

  SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE AND  

  DEMURRER WITH MOTION TO STRIKE 

 

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

 

This is a breach of contract and fraud case.  Plaintiff Martin Kempe alleges that he entered into a written contract with Defendant Leon Gurvin whereby Plaintiff would pay a $6,500 fee and retainer for Gurvin’s attorney, Defendant Michael Bock, in exchange for Gurvin paying Plaintiff half of his recovery in the underlying litigation.  When Gurvin settled his case, Plaintiff claims he refused to give him half the recovery (or $37,500).  

The parties then entered into another contract where Gurvin agreed to pay Kempe $27,000 to settle their dispute.  Bock stated in writing that, “My client has authorized a resolution at 27,000” to settle the dispute.  However, days later, Bock wrote to Plaintiff: “My client (LEON GURVIN) did not find the terms of your client's (MARTIN KEMPE's) proposed settlement agreement acceptable.”   

Plaintiff claims Bock made three misrepresentations of fact: (1) that Gurvin had agreed to settle; (2) that the settlement terms were not acceptable, and (3) that there was a condition to the parties’ agreement involving a Jewish funeral service and burial for Gurvin.  The last misstatement was allegedly made to the Court, in Bock’s demurrer.  Plaintiff claims that Bock made the first two misstatements to help Gurvin flee from the jurisdiction and avoid service of process.   

The operative (second amended) complaint alleges four claims: two breach of contract claims against Gurvin, and fraud and declaratory relief claims against both Gurvin and Bock.  The declaratory relief claim asks the Court to declare that Plaintiff has a corresponding lien against Bock’s IOLTA Account's Attorney Client Trust Funds in the amount of $75,000.00 which Bock is allegedly holding in the name of Gurvin.   

This hearing is on Bock’s special motion to strike and demurrer with motion to strike.  As to the special motion to strike, Bock argues that his settlement communications and arguments in a demurrer are protected activity, and that any claims based on these activities are barred by the litigation privilege.  Bock also filed a demurrer and motion to strike.   

LEGAL STANDARD 

“Litigation of an anti-SLAPP motion involves a two-step process. First, the moving defendant bears the burden of establishing that the challenged allegations or claims arise from protected activity in which the defendant has engaged.  Second, for each claim that does arise from protected activity, the plaintiff must show the claim has “at least ‘minimal merit.’  If the plaintiff cannot make this showing, the court will strike the claim.”  (Bonni v. St. Joseph Health System (2021) 11 Cal.5th 995, 1009.)   

DISCUSSION  

First Prong 

On the first prong, “courts are to consider the elements of the challenged claim and what actions by the defendant supply those elements and consequently form the basis for liability.  The defendant’s burden is to identify what acts each challenged claim rests on and to show how those acts are protected under a statutorily defined category of protected activity.”  (Bonni, 11 Cal.5th at 1009.)  “A defendant need only make a prima facie showing at this stage.”  (Ojjeh v. Brown (2019) 43 Cal.App.5th 1027, 1035–1036.)   

Bock argues that the litigation-related activities in the SAC are protected activities under the anti-SLAPP statute.  The Court agrees.  

In determining what constitutes protected petitioning activity, “we must give adequate ‘breathing space’ to the right of petition.” (Sosa v. DIRECTV, Inc. (9th Cir. 2006) 437 F.3d 923, 932, quoting BE&K Constr. Co. v. NLRB (2002) 536 U.S. 516, 531 [153 L. Ed. 2d 499, 122 S. Ct. 2390].) “The right to petition means more than simply the right to communicate directly with the government. It necessarily includes those activities reasonably and normally attendant to effective petitioning.” (In re IBP Confidential Business Documents Litigation (8th Cir. 1985) 755 F.2d 1300, 1310.)  

Recognized petitioning activities thus include not only the conduct of litigation but also acts and communications reasonably incident to litigation, including prelitigation settlement negotiations. (Takhar v. People ex rel. Feather River Air Quality Management Dist. (2018) 27 Cal.App.5th 15, 28–29; Karnazes v. Ares (2016) 244 Cal.App.4th 344, 353.)   

Further, a defendant’s conduct may be protected petitioning activity even if the statement was not made on the defendant’s own behalf. (Briggs v. Eden Council for Hope & Opportunity (1999) 19 Cal.4th 1106, 1116.) A statement may be entitled to protection if made on behalf of the defendant’s client. (Id.)  Therefore, Bock’s statements to Plaintiff during the parties’ settlement negotiations are protected activity.   

That Plaintiff alleges Bock made false statements in the settlement  negotiations “does not remove them from the definition of protected activity.” (Bonni, 11 Cal.5th at 1025.)  “The protection of the anti-SLAPP statute applies ‘even against allegations of fraudulent promises made during the settlement process’”  (Optional Capital, 18 Cal.App.5th at 114 (citations omitted).) 

As to Bock’s arguments in his demurrer papers, those are also protected activity.  Among other types of communications, the anti-SLAPP statute protects “any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding” (Code Civ. Proc., § 425.16, subd. (e)(1)) or “in connection with an issue under consideration or review” in such proceedings (id., subd. (e)(2)).   

In sum, Bock has met the first prong.  His statements to Plaintiff made on behalf of his client during the parties’ settlement negotiations as well as arguments Bock made in filings before this Court are protected activities.   

Second Prong 

Once a defendant demonstrates that protected conduct is at issue, the plaintiff must show that the complaint is both legally sufficient and supported by a sufficient prima facie showing of facts to sustain a favorable judgment if the evidence submitted by the plaintiff is credited.  (See Navellier v. Sletten (2002) 29 Cal.4th 82, 88-89.)   

“Precisely because the statute (1) permits early intervention in lawsuits alleging unmeritorious causes of action that implicate free speech concerns, and (2) limits opportunity to conduct discovery, the plaintiff’s burden of establishing a probability of prevailing is not high: We do not weigh credibility, nor do we evaluate the weight of the evidence.  Instead, we accept as true all evidence favorable to the plaintiff and assess the defendant’s evidence only to determine if it defeats the plaintiff’s submission as a matter of law. Only a cause of action that lacks ‘even minimal merit’ constitutes SLAPP.”  (Overstock.com, Inc. v. Gradient Analytics, Inc. (2007) 151 Cal.App.4th 688, 699.)  

The SLAPP statute’s second element--a “probability of prevailing”--means a “reasonable probability of prevailing, not prevailing by a preponderance of the evidence.  For this reason, a court must apply a ‘summary-judgment-like’ test, accepting as true the evidence favorable to the plaintiff and evaluating the defendant’s evidence only to determine whether the defendant has defeated the plaintiff’s evidence as a matter of law.”  (Gerbosi v. Gaims, Weil, West & Epstein, LLP (2011) 193 Cal.App.4th 435, 444.) 

Bock argues that the alleged misstatements that form the basis for Plaintiff’s fraud and declaratory relief claims against him are barred by the litigation privilege.  The Court agrees.   

Section 47, subdivision (b), “establishes a privilege that bars liability in tort for the making of certain statements.” (Hagberg v. California Federal Bank (2004) 32 Cal.4th 350, 360.)  Subdivision (b)(3) and (b)(4) confer immunity from civil liability for statements made in any “official proceeding authorized by law” and “the initiation or course of any other proceeding authorized by law…”.  It is an “absolute privilege” and bars all tort causes of action except a claim for malicious prosecution.  (Whelan v. Wolford (1958) 164 Cal.App.2d 689, 694.)  

The litigation privilege “serves broad goals of guaranteeing access to the judicial process, promoting the zealous representation by counsel of their clients, and reinforcing the traditional function of the trial as the engine for the determination of truth. Applying the litigation privilege to some forms of unlawful litigation-related activity may advance those broad goals notwithstanding the occasional unfair result in an individual case.” (Flatley v. Mauro (2006) 39 Cal.4th 299, 324.)   

“To achieve this purpose of curtailing derivative lawsuits, the courts have interpreted the litigation privilege broadly.” (Feldman v. 1100 Park Lane Associates (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 1467, 1485.)  Any doubt about whether the privilege applies is resolved in favor of applying it. (Optional Capital, Inc. v. Akin Gump, Strauss, Hauer & Feld LLP (2017) 18 Cal.App.5th 95, 116.)   

Even fraudulent, perjurious and malicious statements are absolutely privileged so long as they are (1) required or permitted by law, (2) made in a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding, (3) by litigants or other participants authorized by law, (4) to achieve the objects of the litigation, and (5) have some connection or logical relation to the action. (Silberg v. Anderson, supra, 50 Cal.3d at 212; Action Apt. Ass'n, Inc. v. City of Santa Monica (2007) 41 Cal.4th 1232, 1241.) 

Bock’s alleged misrepresentations meet all of these elements.  First, settlement discussions and demurrers are clearly permitted by law.  Second, the alleged misstatements were made in a judicial proceeding or in connection with a judicial proceeding.  Notwithstanding the statutory language “in” a judicial proceeding, Civil Code § 47(b) also protects certain prelawsuit communications such as settlement negotiations. (Edwards v. Centex Real Estate Corp. (1997) 53 Cal.App.4th 15, 34-36; see Hagberg v. California Fed'l Bank FSB (2004) 32 Cal.4th 350, 360-362.)   

Third, the statements achieve the objects of the litigation – settlement and/or dismissal are clearly an object of litigation.  Fourth and last, the statements have some logical relationship to the parties’ dispute.  The settlement communications were designed to resolve the conflict between Gurvin and Plaintiff, and the demurrer was designed to terminate Plaintiff’s action against Bock.   

In sum, both prongs of the anti-SLAPP statute have been met, and the Court will grant the special motion to strike.  As the special motion to strike entirely resolves Plaintiff’s claims against Bock, Bock’s demurrer and motion to strike are now moot.     

CONCLUSION 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS Bock’s special motion to strike the fraud and declaratory relief claims against him.  The Court also OVERRULES Bock’s demurrer and DENIES the motion to strike as moot.

Case Number: 26SMCV01353    Hearing Date: September 22, 2026    Dept: 205

 

 

 

Superior Court of California 

County of Los Angeles – West District  

Beverly Hills Courthouse / Department 205 

 

ALLY BANK,  

 

Plaintiff, 

v. 

 

GERALD JONES, et al.,  

 

Defendants. 

 

  Case No.: 26SMCV01353 

  

  Hearing Date: September 22, 2026 

  [TENTATIVE] order RE: 

  plaintiff’s application for pre- 

  trial writ of possession  

 

 

  

 

 

 

BACKGROUND 

This is a breach of contract case.  Plaintiff Ally Bank is the assignee of a written contract (“Contract”), pursuant to which Defendant Gerald A. Jones aka Gerald Jones bought from the Plaintiff's assignor a used 2021 Tesla Model Y motor vehicle, Vehicle Identification No. 5YJYGDEE4MF099066 (the Tesla).  Plaintiff is the holder of a first priority security interest in the Tesla.   

Defendant defaulted on the Contract by failing to make payments due and owing from February 2, 2025 and thereafter.  The account was charged off on June 30, 2025, and the current balance due and unpaid is $37,353.04, together with other charges as provided in the Contract.  

The Contract provides that upon any default, Plaintiff may take and have immediate possession of the Tesla.  Prior to filing this action, Plaintiff made a demand on Defendant to surrender the Tesla, but Defendant has failed or refused to do so.  At the commencement of this action, the average wholesale value of the Tesla is $20,625, and the average retail value is $24,950.    

The operative complaint alleges two claims for (1) claim and delivery and (2) money on contract.  Under the first cause of action, Plaintiff seeks a pre-trial Writ of Possession directing Defendant to transfer possession of the car to Plaintiff and a Temporary Restraining Order, preventing Defendant from transferring possession of the car, concealing it from Plaintiff, and taking any other action which would harm Plaintiff's interest.  The second cause of action seeks damages of $37,353.04 but less any amounts to be credited to Defendant and less any proceeds of sale should Plaintiff obtain possession of the car.   

This hearing is on Plaintiff’s application for writ of possession and a turnover order.  Plaintiff argues that it has shown a probable validity of prevailing on its cause of action for claim and delivery.  

LEGAL STANDARD 

A¿writ of possession¿is issued as a provisional remedy in a cause of action for claim and delivery, also known as replevin.¿(See¿Pillsbury, Madison & Sutro v. Schectman (1997) 55 Cal.App.4th 1279, 1288.)  This provisional remedy is available in any action in which a plaintiff asserts a present right to the possession of personal property.¿(Costello v. Bell (1915) 27 Cal. App. 102, 104.) 

Generally, a valid writ of possession procedure must include: (1) an opportunity for a pre-seizure hearing, (2) an ex parte seizure in only extraordinary cases; and (3) a showing of probable cause as to both the claim’s validity and to the property’s location. (See 6 Witkin, California Procedure (5th ed. 2008) § 249, pp. 199-200.) 

Upon the filing of the complaint for claim and delivery or replevin, or at any time thereafter, a plaintiff may apply for an order for a writ¿of possession. The parties must use the mandatory approved Judicial Council forms in a claim and delivery proceeding. (Judicial Council Forms CD-100, et seq.). 

At the hearing, the Court decides the merits of the application based on the pleadings and declarations. (Code Civ. Proc., § 512.050.) 

ANALYSIS 

Plaintiff has stated a probable validity of prevailing on its claim for replevin.  The¿elements¿for a¿replevin¿claim are: (1) the plaintiff’s right to possession of the property; (2) the defendant’s wrongful possession; and (3) damages as a result of the wrongful withholding.¿(See 5 Witkin, Cal. Procedure (4th ed. 1997) Pleading, §§ 651-659.)¿ 

Here, Plaintiff has submitted the declaration of its employee, Valerie Molina.  Ms. Molina’s duties include the review of accounts for litigation.  Ms. Molina attests that the Contract is in default, and there is a balance due and owing in the sum of $37,353.04 together with other charges.   

Plaintiff has also identified the location of the Tesla, which is either at 728 W. 124th St., Los Angeles, CA 90044 or 38112 Miramonte Ave. Palmdale, CA 93551.  Plaintiff’s records reflect that Defendant lives at either or both of these addresses.   

As such, the Court grants Plaintiff’s application for writ of possession.  Upon issuance of the writ of possession, the Court may also order Defendant to turn over the Tesla directly to Plaintiff.  Because the¿requirements¿for issuance of the writ of¿possession¿are met, the Court will also issue a turnover order.   

Code Civ. Proc. section 515.010 requires an undertaking to be filed before the writ issues in the amount of “not less than twice the value of the defendant’s interest in the property.”  However, “[i]f the court finds that the defendant has no interest in the property, the court shall waive the requirement of the plaintiff's undertaking and shall include in the order for the issuance of the writ the amount of the defendant's undertaking sufficient to satisfy the requirements of subdivision (b) of Section 515.020.”  (Cal. Code. Civ. Proc. § 515.010(b).) 

In turn, section 515.020(b) provides that a defendant may prevent a successful applicant from taking possession of the subject property, or otherwise regain custody, by filing an undertaking in an amount equal of plaintiff's costs in the action, and “all damages that the plaintiff may sustain by reason of the loss of possession of the property.” 

Here, Plaintiff provides evidence that the amount owed by Defendant (over $37,000) exceeds the market value of the Tesla (between $20,625 and $24,950).  Defendant has no interest in the Tesla pursuant to the Contract.  Thus, no undertaking from Plaintiff is required. 

As to the amount of Defendant’s undertaking, the Court concludes it is the current market value of the Tesla, which is at least $20,625.  Accordingly, in the event Defendant wants to  

prevent Plaintiff from taking possession of the Tesla pursuant to this Court’s writ of possession, he must file an undertaking in the amount of $20,625.   

Plaintiff also seeks to examine Defendant on among other things, the current location of the Tesla in the event it is not at either address indicated in Plaintiff’s application for writ of possession.  The Court grants the request pursuant to Cal. Civ. Proc. Code section 512.050. 

Section 512.050 provides that at the hearing on an application for writ of possession “the court shall make its determinations upon the basis of the pleadings and other papers in the record; but, upon good cause shown, the court may receive and consider additional evidence and authority produced at the hearing or may continue the hearing for the production of such additional evidence, oral or documentary, or the filing of other affidavits or points and authorities.”  Section 512.050, therefore, authorizes the Court to allow the examination of Defendant.   

CONCLUSION 

For the foregoing reasons, the Court GRANTS Plaintiff’s application for writ of possession and issues a turnover order requiring Defendant to turn over to Plaintiff a 2021 Tesla Model Y motor vehicle, Vehicle Identification No. 5YJYGDEE4MF099066.   

 

IT IS SO ORDERED.
